questions.q: What is the typical first step after starting a new Financial Reporting Studio report?
options: Publishing it to the Financial Reporting Center
Adding a grid, then defining its rows
Setting a password for the report
Deleting the GL balances cube
questions.explain: The build sequence starts with adding a grid and defining rows (what you're reporting on) before columns, point of view, and formatting.

questions.q: In the three-line worked example (Total Revenue, Total Expenses, Net Result), what kind of row is "Net Result"?
options: A member pulled directly from the GL balances cube
A formula row, computed as Row 1 minus Row 2
A column, not a row
A point-of-view setting
questions.explain: Net Result is defined as a calculation (Total Revenue minus Total Expenses) rather than a value pulled directly from the cube.

questions.q: If the same three-row, one-column report is rerun with the point of view changed from March to April, what happens?
options: The report must be redesigned from scratch for April
Nothing changes; point of view has no effect on output
The identical design now reports April's numbers instead of March's
The report automatically deletes the March version
questions.explain: This is the core payoff of separating report design from point of view: the same design produces different periods' results depending on the POV selected.

questions.q: Why should a report's title reference point-of-view values rather than hard-coded text like "March 2026"?
options: Hard-coded text runs faster
So the header updates automatically when the period changes, preventing a mismatched heading and data
Oracle Fusion does not allow hard-coded text in headers
It has no real benefit either way
questions.explain: A header that references the point of view updates automatically when the report is rerun for a different period, avoiding an embarrassing mismatch between the heading and the actual data shown.

questions.q: What is the difference between saving a report and publishing it?
options: They are the same action with two different names
Saving keeps the author's work; publishing to a Financial Reporting Center folder is the separate step that makes it visible to its intended audience
Publishing happens automatically the moment you save
Saving requires administrator access; publishing does not
questions.explain: Saving preserves the report for its author, but a separate publish step is required to make it available to other users in the Financial Reporting Center.
